docs.title: VolterraSolution
docs.text:
Below, shape is () (scalar), (d,) (vector) or (d, m) (matrix). The dtype is complex for complex inputs.

Grid output. Each attribute means the same thing in both regimes.

Attribute Shape Sampled Functional t (K,) n·dt, K = N (computed on first access) mesh breakpoints, K = M+1 y (K, *shape) values from D, as today the mesh values, evaluated

Interior breakpoints use the mean convention. y is writable (users subtract exact solutions in place). Invariant: sol(sol.t) equals sol.y to rounding.

Piecewise-polynomial structure. Identical in both regimes; read-only unless noted.

Attribute Shape Meaning mesh (M+1,) breakpoints node_times (M, p) the actual collocation times, stored: on the sampled regime's final interval (Q+r samples) the nodes are snapped to that interval's own grid, so they can't be derived from mesh and nodes node_values (M, p, *shape) the collocation values (the unknowns). Functional: the solve output. Sampled: computed lazily from coefficients. Equals the old callable-family return. coefficients (M, P, *shape) local monomial coefficients in x = (t − tₙ)/hₙ ∈ [0,1]. This is the public accessor the noisy-data residual helper needs. nodes (p,) nominal node positions as floats coll_setting — (divs, [choices]) in the sampled regime, None in the functional regime equation — "vie1", "vie2" or "vide" regime — "sampled" or "functional" continuous — whether the space is C⁰: VIDE, or VIE-1 with continuous=True

Evaluation. - __call__(t, *, at_breakpoints="mean") returns (len(t), *shape), and a scalar t gives a scalar or a shape array (F20, documented). It returns NaN outside [0, T] (F21, documented). - at_breakpoints ∈ {"mean", "left", "right"} and only affects interior breakpoints. - Breakpoints are detected within a few ulps, because n·dt and n·(Q·dt) can differ by one ulp and exact equality would silently fall back to one limit. - At t = 0 only the right limit exists; at t = T only the left. - to_ppoly() returns a scipy.interpolate.PPoly: coefficients cₖ/hₙᵏ, highest degree first, trailing axes shape. That gives derivatives, antiderivatives, integrals and roots. PPoly evaluates right-continuously, and the docstring says so. Complex coefficients must be verified before promising them; if PPoly can't take them, raise TypeError for complex solutions. - __repr__ shows the equation, regime, interval count, T, degree, node set, shape and dtype. - Pickling works; lazy caches are not pickled. Pickles are not promised stable across minor versions; the stability policy says so. - No __len__, indexing, iteration, .polynomials, mesh_breakpoints or from_unit_coefs. These are deprecated aliases in 0.11 only.

Efficiency rules: - Nothing on the default path gets more expensive than today. In the sampled regime y comes from D unchanged. node_values and t are computed on first access. - Dense evaluation: a Horner loop indexing one coefficient at a time (c[idx, k]) instead of today's self._unit[idx] copy. That copy is (len(t), P, *shape), hundreds of MB for a matrix solution on a fine grid. The arithmetic order is unchanged, so the result is bitwise identical. - Coefficients are always produced. The D calls currently skip them when return_polys=False; Phase 7 measures the cost of always asking. I expect it to be negligible, since they are about N·p/Q, versus N for y. - Lazy caches are filled without a lock. That's a benign race, because the computations are idempotent.

docs.title: Shape and matrix-mode rule (F11, F19), stated once
docs.text:
• The time axis comes first.
  • The solution is matrix-valued exactly when some input has a column axis: sampled g (N,d,m), callable g returning (d,m), or y0 (d,m).
  • Every input with a column axis must have the same m.
  • An input without one is shared across all columns. This generalises VIDE's shared-(N,d) forcing to all solvers.
  • Complex inputs give complex outputs, and float32 is upcast.
  • A 2-D kernel array is rejected, which keeps it free for a future non-convolution K(tᵢ, sⱼ) (F25).

docs.title: Kernel convention (F25)
docs.text: A callable kernel is called with one positional array argument u and means K(t − s). A future non-convolution kernel will get a new keyword, never arity sniffing (which breaks on functools.partial, np.vectorize and numba dispatchers). Adding a keyword is non-breaking, so 1.0 only has to not promise arity-based dispatch.

docs.title: 4. Phases
docs.text: Each phase leaves pytest tests/ green, passes the bitwise battery (§5), and ends with an offer to commit. Phases 1–3 change no public signature.

docs.title: Phase 0: contract and baseline
docs.text:
1. Write the contract doc (docs/dev/api-contract-1.0.md; it becomes the user-facing conventions page in Phase 6). It covers:
  2. the regime rule
  3. the shape and matrix rule
  4. the breakpoint convention
  5. the kernel convention and reserved extensions
  6. the type/value error policy (F3: wrong type → TypeError, right type with a wrong value → ValueError; ints are numbers.Integral and not bool; bools must be bool/np.bool_)
  7. the warnings policy
  8. non-finite handling
  9. RuntimeError meaning "internal error, please report" (F4)
  10. the stability policy draft (F31)
  11. Baseline battery: generalise docs/dev/nogc_battery.py into docs/dev/api_battery.py, extended with:
  12. every old-API parameter combination (both families, all three solvers, scalar/vector/runtime-d/matrix/complex, both quadratures, continuous VIE-1, graded meshes, kernel_singularity forms, coll_nodes, a short final interval)

Save the reference from main before Phase 1. compare requires exact equality. 3. Benchmark baseline: run benchmarks/bench_solvers.py locally and keep the JSON. Small-N cases matter here, since the new validation layer is pure overhead there.

docs.title: Phase 1: foundations (no signature changes)
docs.text:
1. _warnings.py: the three classes and _warn(msg, category).
  2. stacklevel is computed by walking frames to the first non-voles frame. That's needed for Python 3.10/3.11; skip_file_prefixes only arrived in 3.12.
  3. Convert all 15 print sites (F1).
  4. show_warnings=False becomes an internal suppress flag checked inside _warn, not warnings.catch_warnings: that mutates process-global state and isn't thread-safe before 3.14, and the matrix path fans out to threads.
  5. The per-column recursive calls (e.g. _col_vie1 → solve_VIE_1 near solvers.py:1299) already pass show_warnings=False. Audit them so every warning is emitted once, from the calling thread (F2).
  6. _validate.py: one helper per parameter kind (integer, positive integer, bool, positive finite real, choice, 1-D increasing finite array starting at 0, array or callable, coll setting, …), each applying the F3 rule. Route _as_int, _check_time_step and friends through it. Behaviour changes, all for the changelog:
  7. coll_divs=2.0 raises TypeError
  8. time_step="0.1" raises a voles TypeError instead of the > comparison error
  9. show_warnings="no" and return_function=1 raise TypeError
  10. Phase 0 bug (a): _resolve_node_pos validates coll_divs as a positive integer (TypeError for 2.5 or 2.0), like the array family's _as_int. F5: soln_init_value=None on VIDE (both families) raises TypeError ("y0 is required").

  12. F6: the finite checks of D12.
  13. F17: move _smooth_gl_order to a module constant (_SMOOTH_GL_ORDER); only src/ uses it.
  14. F24: quadrature accepted case-insensitively.
  15. pytest: set filterwarnings = ["error"] plus explicit ignores, so every warning site must be expected with pytest.warns. Rewrite test_show_warnings.py from capsys to pytest.warns / recwarn, and add a test that a suppressed solve emits nothing from any thread.

Battery: numerics bitwise equal. The expected-exception table is updated only for the deliberate F3/F5 changes, each listed in the commit message.

docs.text:
1. Build VolterraSolution (§3) in _solution.py from today's _SolutionFunction, plus:
  2. the grid output (t, y)
  3. node_times, node_values and the metadata
  4. at_breakpoints with tolerant breakpoint detection
  5. the copy-free Horner loop
  6. to_ppoly(), with complex support verified or refused explicitly
  7. __repr__
  8. 0.11-only deprecated aliases: mesh_breakpoints, polynomials (_polys_from_unit_coefs moves behind it), __getitem__, __iter__, __len__. Keep the legacy _SolutionFunction class unchanged in 0.11 so 0.10 pickles still load; delete it in 1.0.
  9. Internal constructor: VolterraSolution._build(raw, regime, equation, …) takes the cores' _Raw (Phase 3). Until Phase 3 lands, an adapter builds it from today's (values, _SolutionFunction) output.
  10. Tests:
  11. the invariant sol(sol.t) == sol.y (to rounding), in both regimes, for continuous and discontinuous methods
  12. the left/right/mean limits against direct polynomial evaluation
  13. breakpoint detection with ulp-perturbed t

docs.title: Phase 3: separate validation from the cores (no signature changes)
docs.text:
This is the largest internal change. Today each public function validates and computes in one body (solve_VIE_1 is ~390 lines). After this phase:

  1. Move the shared helpers that the callable family imports from solvers.py (_column_workers, _check_vie1_setting, _warn_g_start_columns, _vie1_rho, …; see _callable_solvers.py:30) into _common.py, so neither core imports the other.
  2. git mv solvers.py _sampled.py and git mv _callable_solvers.py _functional.py, which keeps blame intact. voles/solvers.py comes back as a re-export stub; its deprecation is Phase 5.
  3. Split each of the six functions into normalise (validate, apply defaults, determine d/m/complex, produce plain arrays plus (divs, choices) or node_pos) and a core: _sampled_vie1(kernel, g, y0, dt, divs, choices, continuous, quadrature, Q, interp_deg, suppress) -> _Raw and its siblings.
  4. _Raw holds the grid values, unit coefficients, mesh, node times, node values (when the core has them), d and m, so all cores share one return type.
  5. The matrix fan-out and the complex block-embedding stay in the cores, so both API layers get them unchanged.
  6. Apply the D1 private-function renames in the same pass, while every call site is being touched anyway.
  7. The old public functions become normalise-old-kwargs → core → old return shape. This is a pure move. Battery: bitwise, including exception messages.

docs.title: Phase 4: the new API
docs.text:
1. _api.py: solve_vie1/2/vide with full type hints and numpydoc docstrings (Examples sections come in Phase 6).
  2. _classify(kernel, g, a) returns the regime, or a NotImplementedError for mixed inputs. callable() decides: an ndarray is not callable, while Polynomial, scipy interpolators, np.vectorize and numba dispatchers are.
  3. Regime-specific options per §1: dt/coll_setting/quadrature/ samples_per_interval/kernel_interp_degree versus mesh/ coll_nodes/kernel_singularity/reuse_adaptive_blocks. Wrong-regime options raise ValueError naming the regime.
  4. coll_setting resolution (D3): tuple, bare int or None gives (divs, sorted choices), then today's admissibility checks. coll_nodes validated as today.
  5. Shapes per §3 (matrix rule, shared inputs, 2-D kernels rejected).
  6. continuous/y0 per D4.
  7. Call the core and return VolterraSolution._build(...).
  8. Export the new names and warning classes from __init__. Leave the old names in __all__ for 0.11 so from voles import * keeps working.
  9. Tests (new files):
  10. test_api_regimes.py: classification, crossed options, dt≠default with mesh, mixed inputs.
  11. test_api_validation.py: a parametrized table of (call, exception type, message fragment). This makes the F3 policy executable.
  12. test_api_shapes.py: the matrix and shared-input rule across all three solvers and both regimes, plus complex inputs.

  2. array family: sol.y
  3. callable family: sol.node_values

Each emits one DeprecationWarning whose message is the equivalent new call, built from the actual kwargs, e.g. solve_vie2(kernel=..., g=..., dt=0.01, coll_setting=(2, [0, 1, 2])). return_polys and show_warnings keep working inside the wrappers only. 2. fast_coll_settings_* warn through a module-level __getattr__ (F16). There is no public replacement; _supported_coll_settings_d stays private. 3. voles/solvers.py: a stub that warns on import and re-exports the wrappers. 4. optimal_graded_mesh(T=, M=) is accepted with a DeprecationWarning (D1/D10). 5. Tests: - Existing test files keep calling the old API in 0.11. That way the whole legacy suite becomes wrapper coverage, and through the wrappers it exercises the new layer's numerics too. Each such file gets pytestmark = pytest.mark.filterwarnings("ignore::DeprecationWarning"). - New test_legacy_shims.py: every old kwarg is translated, every old return shape is reproduced, and each wrapper warns exactly once per call (not once per column). - The battery passes through the wrappers, bitwise (breakpoints excluded, per D5).

CHANGELOG [0.11.0]: - the new API - the deprecations, with their removal version - the behaviour changes: prints become warnings, the ValueError → TypeError cases, VIDE y0=None, non-finite checks, and dense evaluation at exact breakpoints (mean of the limits) - an announcement that the [callable]/[numba] extras go in 1.0 (F34)

docs.title: 5. Verification and risks
docs.text:
• Bitwise battery (Phase 0 onward) is the main guard: the merge is a re-plumbing, and nothing numerical may move except dense evaluation at exact interior breakpoints (D5). Exception messages are compared too. Phase 3 especially has to keep the old messages exactly.
  • Breakpoint detection tolerance in __call__. Test with t perturbed by ±1–4 ulps, and with t = n·dt versus mesh = arange(M+1)·(Q·dt).
  • Final-interval nodes in the sampled regime: node_times must match snap_nodes exactly. Test with N chosen so that r = 1 and r = Q−1.
  • Warnings and threads: no catch_warnings on the solve path, and warnings are emitted only from the calling thread. test_threading.py gains a "warns once, from the main thread" case.
  • stacklevel must point at the user's call line through every layer (wrapper → API → core). Test it with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) and the recorded filename.
  • Error messages in the new API name new parameters. A wrapper user triggering a validation error sees the new name; the deprecation message printed just before shows the mapping, which is acceptable.
  • to_ppoly() with complex coefficients: verify before documenting.

docs.title: voles 1.0 API contract
docs.text:
Status: DRAFT 2026-10-31 (Phase 0 of docs/dev/api-1.0-plan.md). It becomes the user-facing "Conventions" and "Stability policy" pages in Phase 6.

This document is normative. Anything it promises is covered by the stability policy (§11) from 1.0.0 on, and anything it doesn't promise isn't. Where the implementation disagrees with it, the implementation has a bug or this document needs a decision; it is never silently resolved in favour of the code.

docs.title: 1. Public names
docs.text:
The public API is exactly the names in voles.__all__, their documented parameters and attributes, and voles.__version__:

Name Kind solve_vie1, solve_vie2, solve_vide solver functions VolterraSolution class of the solvers' return value (users never construct it) VolesWarning, AccuracyWarning, PerformanceWarning warning classes optimal_graded_mesh mesh helper gauss_legendre_nodes, radau_iia_nodes, lobatto_nodes node helpers

Anything else is private, including every module (all module names start with an underscore from 1.0), any name starting with an underscore, and the D extension's ABI. Importing the public names from submodules isn't supported; use from voles import ....

docs.title: 2. The three equations
docs.text:
With convolution kernels throughout (§7):

\[\text{VIE-1:}\quad g(t) = \int_0^t K(t-s)\,y(s)\,ds\] \[\text{VIE-2:}\quad y(t) = g(t) + \int_0^t K(t-s)\,y(s)\,ds\] \[\text{VIDE:}\quad y'(t) = a(t)\,y(t) + g(t) + \int_0^t K(t-s)\,y(s)\,ds,\qquad y(0) = y_0\]
  • Every parameter of every public function is keyword-only.
  • g=None means g ≡ 0, and VIDE a=None means a ≡ 0.
  • VIDE y0 is required, and y0=None raises TypeError.

docs.title: 3. Input regimes
docs.text:
Each solve runs in one of two regimes, determined by the types of the data inputs (kernel, g, and for VIDE a):

sampled functional Selected when at least one data input is an array (not callable) and none is callable every data input given is callable Grid dt (sample spacing, default 1.0). Inputs are samples at t = 0, dt, …, (N−1)·dt, where N is the kernel's length. The solver builds a uniform mesh of samples_per_interval samples per interval, with a longer final interval when the samples don't divide evenly. mesh, required: 1-D, finite, strictly increasing, mesh[0] == 0 Node set coll_setting (§5.1) coll_nodes (§5.2) Options that apply only here coll_setting, quadrature, samples_per_interval, kernel_interp_degree mesh, coll_nodes, kernel_singularity, reuse_adaptive_blocks

Rules:

  1. "Callable" means callable(x) is true. NumPy arrays are not callable; functions, numpy.polynomial.Polynomial, scipy interpolators, np.vectorize objects and numba dispatchers are.
  2. Mixed inputs (some data inputs callable, some arrays) raise NotImplementedError. The combination is reserved (§7), and its message says so.
  3. An option belonging to the other regime raises ValueError naming the inferred regime and the reason. That includes mesh in the sampled regime, coll_setting in the functional regime, and a dt other than the default in the functional regime. An explicit dt=1.0 alongside mesh is indistinguishable from the default and is ignored.
  4. VolterraSolution.regime records the regime (§8).

docs.title: 4. Solver signatures
docs.text:
```python notest solve_vie1(*, kernel, g=None, continuous=False, y0=None, dt=1.0, coll_setting=None, quadrature="product", samples_per_interval=None, kernel_interp_degree=None, mesh=None, coll_nodes=None, kernel_singularity=None, reuse_adaptive_blocks=True) -> VolterraSolution

solve_vie2(*, kernel, g=None, dt=1.0, coll_setting=None, quadrature="product", samples_per_interval=None, kernel_interp_degree=None, mesh=None, coll_nodes=None, kernel_singularity=None, reuse_adaptive_blocks=True) -> VolterraSolution

solve_vide(*, kernel, a=None, g=None, y0, dt=1.0, coll_setting=None, quadrature="product", samples_per_interval=None, kernel_interp_degree=None, mesh=None, coll_nodes=None, kernel_singularity=None, reuse_adaptive_blocks=True) -> VolterraSolution ```

VIE-1 method choice. - continuous=False (default): the discontinuous collocation space S⁽⁻¹⁾ₘ₋₁. Passing y0 then raises ValueError. - continuous=True: the continuous space S⁽⁰⁾ₘ, which needs the initial value: y0 is required (ValueError if missing). - The two methods admit different node sets (§5.3).

docs.title: 5.1 Sampled regime: coll_setting
docs.text:
Value Meaning None the default: VIE-1 (3, [1, 2, 3]); VIE-2 and VIDE (2, [0, 1, 2]) divs (int) every point the method admits: (divs, [1, …, divs]) for VIE-1, (divs, [0, …, divs]) otherwise (divs, choices) nodes cᵢ = choicesᵢ/divs; any length-2 sequence
  • divs is a positive integer. choices is a non-empty sequence of distinct integers in 0..divs (1..divs for VIE-1), in any order, and is sorted internally.
  • Python and NumPy integers are accepted. bool, floats (even integer-valued ones) and other types raise TypeError.
  • divs is not only the nodes' denominator: it also fixes the mesh (samples_per_interval below). Settings with the same node positions but different divs are different methods.

Mesh width (samples_per_interval, Q):

quadrature Allowed Q Default "product" (default) any positive multiple of divs divs² for VIE-1; divs for VIE-2 and VIDE "collocation" exactly divs² divs²
  • The VIE-1 default is wider because inverting a first-kind equation amplifies data errors by about the inverse of the mesh width. The Conventions page will carry a worked example of the trade-off.
  • kernel_interp_degree (default: the number of nodes) applies only to quadrature="product". With "collocation" it raises ValueError.
  • quadrature is matched case-insensitively.
  • The kernel needs at least Q+1 samples.

docs.title: 5.2 Functional regime: coll_nodes
docs.text:
• A non-empty 1-D sequence of distinct finite floats in [0, 1] ((0, 1] for VIE-1), in any order, sorted internally.
  • None gives the same positions as the sampled default: VIE-1 {1/3, 2/3, 1}; VIE-2 and VIDE {0, 1/2, 1}.
  • The node helpers return valid arrays, e.g. coll_nodes=voles.radau_iia_nodes(3).

docs.title: 5.3 Admissibility
docs.text:
• VIE-1 node sets must give a convergent method: |ρ| ≤ 1 with ρ = (−1)ᵐ ∏ (1 − cᵢ)/cᵢ for the discontinuous method, and the product over i < m for the continuous one. Otherwise ValueError.
  • The continuous method also requires c_m = 1.
  • ρ = +1 is admitted at one order lower, with an AccuracyWarning. A bare divs with continuous=True gives ρ = (−1)^divs, so this happens for even divs.
  • The ρ test is the only VIE-1 admissibility rule. It is evaluated exactly in rational arithmetic in the sampled regime, and in floating point for coll_nodes.
  • Only quadrature="collocation" depends on which settings are compiled into the extension (divs ≤ 4 in current builds); "product" accepts every valid setting. An uncompiled setting under "collocation":
  • scalar problems run on the numba fallback with a PerformanceWarning when numba is installed, and raise NotImplementedError otherwise;
  • vector and matrix problems raise NotImplementedError.

Both messages suggest quadrature="product". (Today's messages don't, and the scalar one points to fast_coll_settings_*; Phase 4 rewrites them.)

docs.title: 6. Shapes and dtypes
docs.text:
Time axis first, always. "Component shape" cs is () for scalar, (d,) for vector and (d, m) for matrix problems.

Input Sampled Functional (return value of the callable) kernel (N,) scalar, (N, d, d) vector/matrix K(u) → scalar or (d, d) g (N,), (N, d), (N, d, m) g(t) → scalar, (d,), (d, m) a (VIDE) (N,) or (N, d, d) a(t) → scalar or (d, d) y0 scalar, (d,), (d, m) the same
  • Matrix mode. The problem is matrix-valued exactly when some input has a column axis (g of (N, d, m) or (d, m), or y0 of (d, m)). Every input with a column axis must have the same m. An input without one is shared by all m columns. The columns are independent problems with a common kernel; they may be solved in parallel threads.
  • Callables must accept a scalar argument. The kernel is also tried with a 1-D array, and if it returns the leading-axis-stacked results it is used vectorised, which is much faster. g and a are currently called pointwise; a future release may vectorise them the same way, detected rather than assumed. Return shapes are detected by sampling.
  • Complex. Complex inputs (or callables returning complex values) give a complex solution. Real inputs give a real solution.
  • dtypes. Integer and float32 inputs are converted to float64 (or complex128). The output dtype is float64 or complex128.
  • Rejected arrays. A 2-D sampled kernel is invalid (reserved, §7). A sampled kernel of (N, d, d') with d ≠ d′ is invalid.
  • Non-finite values.
  • Arrays containing NaN or ±inf raise ValueError, naming the input and the first bad index.
  • Callable g and a are checked at the collocation times, with the same error.
  • Callable kernels are not checked: a weakly singular kernel legitimately returns inf at u = 0, which the quadrature never samples. Non-finite kernel values elsewhere give non-finite results.

docs.title: 7. Kernel convention and reserved extensions
docs.text:
• A callable kernel is called with one positional argument u (a scalar or 1-D array) and means K(t − s) evaluated at u = t − s ≥ 0. Kernel arity is never inspected.
  • Reserved, not promised. The following may be added in 1.x without breaking anything:
  • Non-convolution kernels K(t, s), through a new keyword argument. A 2-D sampled kernel is invalid in 1.0 so that it can carry this meaning later.
  • Mixed inputs: e.g. an analytic, possibly singular kernel with a sampled forcing, on the sample grid with coll_setting. These raise NotImplementedError in 1.0.
  • Iterated solutions: an iterated keyword for solve_vie2 and solve_vide, returning the iterated collocation solution u_it(t) = g(t) + ∫₀ᵗ K(t−s) uₕ(s) ds (and the VIDE analogue). The name iterated is reserved.
  • kernel_singularity declares weak singularities of the kernel (functional regime only). It accepts None, a location, a list of locations, a dict {location: alpha}, or a callable t ↦ locations; bools are rejected.
  • Locations in the first three forms are in u = t − s. In the dict form a non-None alpha ∈ (0, 1) declares K ∼ |u − u₀|^(−α) and enables Gauss–Jacobi rules.
  • The callable returns s-locations for collocation time t (an Abel kernel is lambda t: [t]), which anticipates non-convolution kernels.

docs.text: The solvers return a VolterraSolution, a continuous or discontinuous piecewise polynomial on mesh. Users don't construct it.

docs.title: 8.3 Evaluation
docs.text:
sol(t, *, at_breakpoints="mean"):

  • Shapes. A scalar t returns a Python float or complex for scalar problems and an ndarray of shape cs otherwise. An array t returns (*t.shape, *cs).
  • Domain. t ∈ [0, T] up to a rounding-level tolerance; points outside return NaN, never extrapolated values.
  • Breakpoints. At an interior breakpoint the two one-sided limits of a discontinuous solution differ. at_breakpoints chooses "mean" (the default), "left" or "right". A point within a few ulps of a breakpoint counts as that breakpoint. At t = 0 and t = T only one limit exists and is used.
  • Choosing a convention. "mean" is the most accurate of the three for most node sets. With VIE-2 and c_m = 1 (e.g. Radau IIA), "left" is superconvergent and better. The Conventions page carries the measured table.

sol.to_ppoly() returns an equivalent scipy.interpolate.PPoly (trailing axes cs). It is right-continuous at breakpoints and can differentiate, integrate and find roots. Complex solutions are supported if and only if PPoly supports them (to be verified in Phase 2; otherwise TypeError).

docs.title: 8.4 Other behaviour
docs.text:
• repr(sol) is a one-line summary. Its exact text isn't part of the contract.
  • Solutions pickle. Pickles are not guaranteed to load in a different minor version.
  • No len(), indexing or iteration.

docs.title: 9. Errors
docs.text:
Exception When TypeError an argument has the wrong type, e.g. a float where an int is required, a non-bool flag, a non-callable where a callable is required in the functional regime, a non-numeric array, y0=None where y0 is required. Python's own TypeError for unknown or missing keywords. ValueError the type is right but the value is not: shapes, ranges, signs, inadmissible node sets, options from the other regime, inputs too short for the mesh, non-finite data, conflicting arguments NotImplementedError mixed inputs (§3); a setting that isn't compiled with no fallback for that problem shape (§5.3) numpy.linalg.LinAlgError a collocation system is singular or numerically singular ImportError the D extension can't be found or loaded RuntimeError an internal error. It always indicates a bug in voles, and its message asks for a report.
  • Type versus value rule. Integers are numbers.Integral but not bool. Flags are bool or numpy.bool_. Reals are numbers.Real but not bool. Arrays are anything numpy.asarray turns into a numeric array.
  • Integers aren't coerced. Floats are never truncated to ints (2.0 is a TypeError where an int is required), because silently running a different discretisation is worse than an error.
  • Messages name the offending parameter by its public name and, where useful, its value and the expected form. Message text isn't part of the contract.

docs.title: 10. Warnings
docs.text:
Class Base Emitted for VolesWarning UserWarning base class; also: kernel_singularity locations outside [0, T] AccuracyWarning VolesWarning ρ = +1 order reduction; VIE-1 with g(0) ≠ 0; VIE-1 with K(0) small or singular under collocation quadrature; a declared singularity on a uniform mesh PerformanceWarning VolesWarning the numba fallback; an extension build lacking a fast path
  • Warnings are emitted with warnings.warn. Each points at the user's call, is emitted at most once per solve call, and comes from the calling thread, never a worker thread.
  • warnings.simplefilter("ignore", voles.VolesWarning) silences all of them. "error" turns them into exceptions.
  • voles never prints. Third-party warnings (e.g. scipy's IntegrationWarning from adaptive quadrature) pass through unchanged.
  • The set of conditions that warn may grow in a minor release; new warnings are always VolesWarning subclasses.

docs.title: 11. Stability policy (from 1.0.0)
docs.text:
voles follows semantic versioning on the public API of §1.

  • Major releases may remove or incompatibly change public names, parameters, defaults, return types or attributes.
  • Minor releases may:
  • add names, keyword parameters with defaults, attributes and warning conditions;
  • change numerical results only as a documented accuracy or robustness improvement, named in the changelog;
  • deprecate. Deprecated features emit DeprecationWarning for at least one minor release before removal in the next major release.
  • Patch releases fix bugs only. A fix may change a result that was wrong.
  • Not covered: private names, message text, repr text, pickles across minor versions, the D ABI, performance (though regressions are treated as bugs), and bitwise reproducibility across platforms or builds.
  • Supported Python versions follow the classifiers in pyproject.toml. Dropping a Python version that is past end-of-life is allowed in a minor release.

docs.title: 12. Threads
docs.text:
• Solver calls are thread-safe. Concurrent calls from different Python threads give the same results as serial calls.
  • The extension releases the GIL during compiled work (ctypes.CDLL).
  • Matrix-mode solves may use a thread pool internally, sized to the column count and the CPU count.

docs.title: 13. Transition (0.11 only; removed in 1.0)
docs.text:
• 0.11.0 keeps solve_VIE_1, solve_VIE_2, solve_VIDE, function_solve_VIE_1, function_solve_VIE_2, function_solve_VIDE, fast_coll_settings_* and voles.solvers as deprecated wrappers.
  • They return their 0.10 types.
  • Their numerics are bitwise identical to 0.10, except for dense evaluation at exact interior breakpoints (now the mean of the limits).
  • Changes that affect 0.10 code directly, all listed in the 0.11 changelog:
  • warnings instead of prints
  • TypeError for wrong-type arguments
  • y0=None rejected in VIDE
  • non-finite data rejected
  • The migration table is in docs/dev/api-1.0-plan.md, Appendix A, and becomes the "Migration from 0.10" page.

docs.title: Part 2 — Findings
docs.text: Severity: A = would block a 1.0 at NumPy/SciPy review standard; B = should fix before 1.0, breaking changes need a deprecation cycle; C = polish, can follow 1.0.

docs.title: Lens 1: Error and warning model
docs.text:
F1 (A). Warnings are print() statements. Fifteen diagnostic sites write "warning: ..." to stdout. They cannot be filtered, promoted to errors, captured in tests, or silenced per category; show_warnings=False is the only control and it is all-or-nothing. In a Jupyter cell or a batch job the message is invisible or lost. Proposed: define VolesWarning(UserWarning) with two or three subclasses (e.g. ConvergenceWarning for ρ = 1, g(0) ≠ 0, K(0) small; PerformanceWarning for the Numba fallback and the stale-extension notice; MeshWarning for the uniform-mesh hint) and emit through warnings.warn(..., stacklevel=2). Then deprecate show_warnings (see F2).

F2 (B). show_warnings duplicates the standard warnings machinery. Once F1 is done, show_warnings=False is warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=VolesWarning). Keep the parameter through 1.0 as a convenience if you like, but define it as exactly that filter so the two can never disagree. SciPy has no such flag on any solver.

F3 (B). ValueError is used where TypeError belongs. coll_divs=2.0, coll_choices=[0.5], order=1.5, p=2.0 all raise ValueError for what is a type problem. Python convention and NumPy/SciPy practice: wrong type → TypeError, right type wrong value → ValueError. Conversely time_step="0.1" escapes validation and raises TypeError: '>' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'float' from the comparison. show_warnings="no" and return_function=1 are accepted without comment. Decide the rule once (a one-line policy in the contract doc) and apply it in a single _validate helper per parameter.

F4 (B). RuntimeError from the D extension is undocumented. _dlang.py:246 raises RuntimeError(f"{func_name} returned error code {ret}"). No docstring lists it, and the message is not actionable for a user. Either map the known codes to the documented exceptions or document it.

F5 (B). soln_init_value=None on solve_VIDE silently produces an all-NaN solution. _scalar_init(None) goes through np.asarray(None, dtype=float) → nan. The parameter is documented as required and is required syntactically, but an explicit None (easy to produce from a config dict) is accepted. Should raise.

F6 (C). NaN and inf in the data propagate silently. kernel_values or g_values containing NaN/inf yield an all-NaN result with no diagnostic. The tests codify "raises or propagates". SciPy's solve_ivp and quad do not check either, so this is defensible, but the Raises section should say so explicitly ("non-finite input is not checked"), or a cheap np.isfinite check should raise ValueError.

docs.title: Lens 2: Consistency across the six solvers
docs.text:
F7 (A). The two families name the same concept differently.

Concept array family callable family kernel kernel_values kernel forcing g_values g coefficient a_values a time grid time_step (+ implicit N) mesh_breakpoints initial value soln_init_value soln_init_value node set coll_divs, coll_choices coll_divs, coll_choices, coll_nodes

The _values suffix is justified for the array family only because the same names mean callables elsewhere. A single family with kernel= accepting either an array or a callable (dispatch on callable(kernel)) would remove the prefix function_ and the suffix _values together. See F9 before deciding.

F8 (A). coll_divs means two different things in the two families. Array family: a mesh interval is coll_divs**2 samples (collocation quadrature) or mesh_samples samples, with coll_divs sub-intervals. Callable family: coll_divs only sets node positions k/coll_divs; the mesh is mesh_breakpoints. The docs flag this in a "Convention note" because it bites. For 1.0 the node set should be expressed one way everywhere. The callable family's coll_nodes (floats in [0,1]) is the general form; coll_divs/coll_choices is a rational special case of it. Proposed: a single nodes= parameter accepting an array of floats in [0,1] or a string preset ("radau", "gauss", "lobatto", "uniform") with a count, and coll_divs/coll_choices kept only as the array family's sampling parameter under a name that says so (e.g. samples_per_interval).

F9 (A). The two families return different things for "the solution". Array family: values at the input sample times, shape (N, ...). Callable family: values at the collocation nodes, shape (M, p, ...), and no time array. A user of function_solve_* must reconstruct t[n, i] = mesh[n] + c_i * h_n themselves; the docs example does exactly this in a double loop. This is the strongest argument for a result object (F10): res.t and res.y make both families return the same thing, and res.sol is the dense output.

F10 (A). The solution object is a private class with no public name and no repr. type(solution) is voles._solution._SolutionFunction; repr is the default. Users cannot annotate it, isinstance it, or document it. Proposed: a public VolterraResult (or VolterraSolution) modelled on scipy.integrate.OdeResult: attributes t, y, sol (the callable), mesh, nodes, method-style metadata, success/message if you ever add adaptive failure modes, and a useful __repr__. Then return_function is unnecessary: the callable is always available (coefficient storage is already cheap; the Polynomial list is lazy).

F11 (B). Matrix mode is selected by different inputs in different solvers. VIE-1/VIE-2: 3-D g_values. VIDE: 2-D soln_init_value (3-D g_values alone does not select it). Callable VIE-1/2: 2-D return from g. This is documented but asymmetric. With a result object and explicit shapes it is better to select on one rule: trailing axis of g (or y0 where g is absent).

F12 (B). VIE-1's soln_init_value is a conditional parameter with a printed warning when ignored. It only means anything with force_continuous=True. Two parameters that are only valid together is a smell; consider continuous=y0 (None = discontinuous method, a value = continuous method with that initial value), which removes the warning and the "required when" clause.

docs.title: Lens 3: Naming
docs.text:
F13 (B). soln_init_value → y0. Every ODE/IE interface in SciPy, Julia, and MATLAB calls this y0. The equations in the docstrings already write y(0) = y_0.

F14 (B). function_solve_* prefix. Reads as "the function that solves" rather than "solve from functions". If the families stay separate, solve_VIE_2_callable or a callable/sampled keyword is clearer; if merged (F7), the prefix disappears.

F15 (C). VIE_1 / VIE_2 / VIDE casing. Mixed case in function names is non-PEP8 and unusual in NumPy/SciPy (solve_ivp, solve_bvp). solve_vie1, solve_vie2, solve_vide would be conventional. This is a judgement call; the current names are at least internally consistent and searchable. Decide and record it.

F16 (B). fast_coll_settings_* expose a build detail as API. The lists answer "which settings run compiled under quadrature="collocation"", a question that disappeared from the default path in 0.10. They also have an awkward type (list of (int, list)). Either drop them from __all__ (keep as voles.compiled_settings() returning a frozenset, undocumented in the main nav) or deprecate them outright.

F17 (C). _smooth_gl_order in the public signature. A leading-underscore parameter appears in help(), the rendered API pages, and inspect.signature. Move it to a module-level knob or **_internal.

F18 (C). optimal_graded_mesh parameter names. alpha, T, M, order are fine for the audience but inconsistent with the solvers' verbosity (mesh_breakpoints, soln_init_value). n_intervals for M would match. Low priority.

docs.title: Lens 4: Return types and dtype/shape contract
docs.text:
F19 (B). No single written statement of the shape contract. Shapes are scattered across six docstrings. Needed once, in the user guide: time axis first; scalar (), vector (d,), matrix (d, m); kernel (d, d); complex handled by block embedding; float32 upcast; no broadcasting of g against columns except the documented shared-(N, d) case for VIDE. The review found one undocumented asymmetry: VIDE accepts a shared (N, d) forcing for all columns, VIE-1/2 do not.

F20 (C). Scalar solution(t) returns a Python float, array t returns ndarray. Matches np.polynomial.Polynomial behaviour, so acceptable, but say so.

F21 (C). Dense output outside [0, T] is NaN rather than an error. Reasonable and documented. SciPy's OdeSolution extrapolates silently, which is worse. Keep.

docs.title: Lens 5: Defaults and inference
docs.text:
F22 (B). Three different defaults for "what happens when I give only one of coll_divs/coll_choices". The rules (coll_divs alone → all points; coll_choices alone → max entry; neither → (3,[1,2,3]) or (2,[0,1,2])) are sensible and now documented, but they are a consequence of the two-integer encoding. Under F8 they vanish.

F23 (B). Default mesh_samples differs between VIE-1 (coll_divs**2) and VIE-2/VIDE (coll_divs). Justified in the Notes (first-kind amplification), but a researcher comparing a first- and second-kind solve on the same data gets different mesh widths without asking. Fine to keep; needs one sentence in the user guide and a worked example of the trade-off.

F24 (C). quadrature is case-sensitive and the error lists the options. Fine. Consider accepting str.lower().

docs.title: Lens 6: Extensibility
docs.text:
F25 (B). Non-convolution kernels are the announced next feature and the current signatures leave no slot for them. kernel(u) and kernel_values[(N,)] both assume K(t - s). The callable kernel_singularity form already anticipates K(t, s). If 1.0 ships before that feature, the contract doc should reserve the extension (e.g. kernel of two arguments detected by arity, or a convolution: bool flag) so it is not a breaking change later.

F26 (C). quadrature= and coll_nodes= are good extension points. Keyword-only everywhere is good. No positional parameters exist except p in the node helpers, which is fine.

docs.title: Lens 7: Documentation contract
docs.text:
F27 (B). Docstrings have no Examples section and nothing is doctested. optimal_graded_mesh has a non-runnable example with .... SciPy requires a runnable example on every public function and runs them in CI. The pytest-markdown-docs dev dependency suggests the docs pages are tested; the docstrings are not.

F28 (B). Cross-references use double backticks rather than numpydoc's single-backtick role. See ``function_solve_VIE_2``` renders as literal text, not a link, under mkdocstrings. Use ``function_solve_VIE_2`` and addSee Also` sections.

F29 (C). Raises sections list ValueError once with a paragraph of causes. Acceptable, but once F3 lands, split TypeError from ValueError and list RuntimeError (F4) and VolesWarning subclasses under a Warns section.

F30 (C). Type hints are partial and py.typed is absent. The array family has none; the callable family has int = None. For 1.0 either annotate everything and ship py.typed, or strip the partial hints so they do not mislead.

docs.title: Lens 8: Packaging and stability
docs.text:
F31 (A). No written stability or deprecation policy. Nothing in README, CHANGELOG, or CONTRIBUTING says what 1.0 promises. One paragraph: semver on the public names in __all__; numerical results may change in a minor release only when the change is a documented accuracy improvement; deprecations warn for at least one minor release.

F32 (B). No signature-snapshot test. A test that pins inspect.signature of every public callable, and the set of names in __all__, catches accidental breaks from then on.

F33 (C). __version__ comes from installed metadata. Correct for wheels, misleading for editable installs with stale metadata (this checkout reports 0.7.0 from a 0.10.0 source tree). Hatch can write a _version.py at build time; either is fine, just be aware.

F34 (C). [callable] and [numba] extras are redundant with [full]. Already noted as compatibility shims in pyproject.toml. Drop at 1.0.

docs.title: Part 3 — Suggested shape of the 1.0 surface
docs.text:
Not a decision, a strawman to argue with. It resolves F7–F14 and F19 at once.

python notest res = voles.solve_vie2( kernel, # array (N,) / (N,d,d) sampled at t = 0, h, ..., or callable K(u) g=None, # array or callable, same convention as kernel t=None, # float h (uniform sampling) or 1-D mesh breakpoints nodes="radau", # str preset, or array of floats in [0, 1], or (divs, choices) order=3, # number of nodes when `nodes` is a preset singularity=None, # as today's kernel_singularity quadrature="product", mesh_samples=None, kernel_interp_degree=None, ) res.t # times where res.y is reported (sample times, or collocation nodes) res.y # values, shape (len(t), ...) — time axis first, always res.sol # callable dense output, NaN outside [0, T] res.mesh # breakpoints res.nodes # node positions in [0, 1]

solve_vie1 adds continuous=None (a y0 value turns on the continuous method); solve_vide adds a=None and required y0. Everything today's API does is reachable; the six functions become three; return_function, return_polys, show_warnings, soln_init_value, force_continuous, coll_divs, coll_choices, coll_nodes, function_solve_*, and fast_coll_settings_* become deprecation shims for one minor release.

If merging the families is too large a change, the minimum set that still reaches the bar is: F1, F3, F5, F9, F10, F13, F31, F32 — a result object with t/y/sol, real warnings, a type/value error rule, y0, and a policy.

docs.title: Example: Complex-Valued Equations
docs.text:
Both solver families accept complex-valued inputs. Pass complex NumPy arrays for the kernel, forcing function, and (for VIDE) initial value, and the solver returns a complex-valued solution. This works for scalar, vector, and matrix cases alike (and for the callable-input family too — pass callables that return complex values).

import numpy as np
from voles import solve_VIE_2

time_step = 0.05
times = np.arange(0, 2.05, time_step)      # 41 points = 10×2² + 1
kernel = np.exp(-1j * times)               # complex kernel
g = np.ones_like(times, dtype=complex)

soln = solve_VIE_2(kernel_values=kernel, g_values=g, time_step=time_step)
# soln is a complex-valued array
print(soln.dtype)

docs.title: Example: Callable-input solvers with arbitrary mesh
docs.text:
The function_solve_* family accepts callable kernel(u), g(t), and a(t) instead of pre-sampled arrays, supports arbitrary mesh_breakpoints, and handles integrable singularities in the kernel.

Convention note: unlike the array-based solvers, mesh_breakpoints here defines the integration intervals directly. coll_divs only controls where collocation nodes sit within each interval (at fractional positions coll_choices[k] / coll_divs), not sub-division. Pass more breakpoints for finer resolution.

docs.title: Smooth kernel, arbitrary mesh
docs.text:
The same problem as the standard VIE-2 example, but expressed with callables and a hand-picked non-uniform mesh:

import numpy as np
from voles import function_solve_VIE_2

kernel = lambda u: np.exp(-u)
g = lambda t: 0.5 * (np.sin(t) + np.cos(t) - np.exp(-t))  # exact y(t) = sin(t)

# Non-uniform mesh: more resolution where g is changing fastest
mesh = np.array([0.0, 0.05, 0.12, 0.22, 0.35, 0.50, 0.68, 0.85, 1.0])

y_arr, y = function_solve_VIE_2(
    kernel=kernel, g=g, mesh_breakpoints=mesh,
    coll_divs=2, coll_choices=[0, 1, 2],
    return_function=True,
)

print(y(0.37), "vs exact", np.sin(0.37))
print("max nodal error:", np.max(np.abs(y(np.linspace(0, 1, 100))
                                        - np.sin(np.linspace(0, 1, 100)))))

y is a callable object: evaluate at any scalar or array of times. The underlying per-interval polynomials are available as y.polynomials.

docs.title: Weakly singular kernel + graded mesh
docs.text:
For Abel-type kernels \(K(u) \sim u^{-\alpha}\), declaring the singularity and using optimal_graded_mesh recovers full collocation convergence order that a uniform mesh fails to achieve.

import numpy as np
from voles import function_solve_VIE_2, optimal_graded_mesh

# Classical Abel equation: integral of (t-s)^(-1/2) y(s) ds = pi*t/2  =>  y = sqrt(t)
kernel = lambda u: 1.0 / np.sqrt(u) if u > 0 else 0.0
g = lambda t: np.sqrt(t) - 0.5 * np.pi * t

coll_choices = [0, 1, 2]
mesh = optimal_graded_mesh(alpha=0.5, T=1.0, M=30, order=len(coll_choices))

y_arr = function_solve_VIE_2(
    kernel=kernel, g=g,
    mesh_breakpoints=mesh,
    coll_divs=2, coll_choices=coll_choices,
    kernel_singularity=0.0,   # declare the singularity at u=0
)

# Check accuracy at the collocation nodes
node_pos = np.array([0, 1, 2]) / 2.0
err = 0.0
for n in range(len(mesh) - 1):
    h = mesh[n + 1] - mesh[n]
    for i, c in enumerate(node_pos):
        t = mesh[n] + c * h
        err = max(err, abs(y_arr[n, i] - np.sqrt(t)))
print(f"max error: {err:.2e}")

Declaring the singularity matters: the quadrature nodes are all interior, so an undeclared endpoint singularity usually does not raise an error — the solver quietly loses convergence order (and spends longer in adaptive fallbacks) instead. If the kernel ever evaluates to inf/nan at a quadrature node, a ValueError from the weight tensor's np.isfinite check points you to kernel_singularity, but do not rely on that safety net: declare every integrable singularity you know about. (The solver also emits a voles.AccuracyWarning if you declare a singularity on a near-uniform mesh, suggesting optimal_graded_mesh; silence it with show_warnings=False or a warnings filter.)

docs.title: Known power law? Declare it for a much faster build
docs.text:
If you also know the singularity's exponent, use the dict form kernel_singularity={location: alpha} for \(K(u) \sim |u - u_0|^{-\alpha}\). Blocks touching the singularity are then integrated by deterministic Gauss–Jacobi rules with the singular factor absorbed into the quadrature weight — on the Abel problem above this makes the weight-tensor build several times faster on a graded mesh, and an order of magnitude faster on a uniform mesh (where the deterministic rules can be reused across the Toeplitz assembly), with the same accuracy:

import numpy as np
from voles import function_solve_VIE_2, optimal_graded_mesh

kernel = lambda u: 1.0 / np.sqrt(u) if u > 0 else 0.0
g = lambda t: np.sqrt(t) - 0.5 * np.pi * t   # exact y = sqrt(t)
mesh = optimal_graded_mesh(alpha=0.5, T=1.0, M=30, order=3)

y_arr = function_solve_VIE_2(
    kernel=kernel, g=g,
    mesh_breakpoints=mesh,
    coll_divs=2, coll_choices=[0, 1, 2],
    kernel_singularity={0.0: 0.5},   # K(u) ~ u^(-1/2) near u = 0
)

A wrongly declared exponent is caught by a two-order acceptance check and falls back to the adaptive treatment automatically, so the dict form is never less accurate than the location-only form. Relatedly, on uniform meshes the reuse_adaptive_blocks=True flag speeds up the location-only (adaptive) path by reusing adaptive blocks across the Toeplitz assembly, at the price of deviations from the default path bounded by the quadrature tolerance (~1e-8); with a fully declared dict form it is unnecessary (a no-op).

docs.title: Choosing collocation nodes directly
docs.text:
Instead of the rational coll_divs/coll_choices grid, nodes can be given directly with coll_nodes — including the classical families via the gauss_legendre_nodes, radau_iia_nodes, and lobatto_nodes helpers:

import numpy as np
from voles import function_solve_VIE_2, gauss_legendre_nodes

kernel = lambda u: np.exp(-u)
g = lambda t: 0.5 * (np.sin(t) + np.cos(t) - np.exp(-t))  # exact y(t) = sin(t)

y_arr = function_solve_VIE_2(
    kernel=kernel, g=g, mesh_breakpoints=np.linspace(0, 1, 21),
    coll_nodes=gauss_legendre_nodes(3),   # superconvergent for VIE-2/VIDE
)

Gauss–Legendre nodes give mesh-point superconvergence for VIE-2 and VIDE; for VIE-1 prefer radau_iia_nodes (the right-endpoint node gives the full collocation order — see the function_solve_VIE_1 API notes on convergence).

docs.title: Vector-valued kernel
docs.text:
Pass a kernel(u) that returns a (d, d) matrix; g(t) returns (d,):

import numpy as np
from voles import function_solve_VIE_2

d = 2
identity = np.eye(d)
# np.multiply.outer gives a (d, d) matrix for scalar u and an (n, d, d) stack
# for an array of u values; the solver then assembles the weights of a whole
# mesh row in one call. (np.exp(-u) * identity would only accept scalars and
# runs several times slower.)
kernel = lambda u: np.multiply.outer(np.exp(-u), identity)
g_s = lambda t: 0.5 * (np.sin(t) + np.cos(t) - np.exp(-t))
g = lambda t: np.array([g_s(t), g_s(t)])

mesh = np.linspace(0, 1, 21)
y_arr, y = function_solve_VIE_2(
    kernel=kernel, g=g, mesh_breakpoints=mesh,
    coll_divs=2, coll_choices=[0, 1, 2],
    return_function=True,
)

# y(t) returns (d,); y(array) returns (len(array), d)
print(y(0.5).shape)             # (2,)
print(y(np.linspace(0, 1, 5)).shape)  # (5, 2)

docs.title: Matrix-valued: many right-hand sides at once
docs.text:
To solve several right-hand sides that share the same kernel, return a (d, m) array from g(t) (and, for function_solve_VIDE, pass a (d, m) soln_init_value). The kernel weight tensor — the expensive part to build — is computed once and reused across all m columns, so this is much cheaper than m separate calls.

import numpy as np
from voles import function_solve_VIE_2

d = 2
identity = np.eye(d)
kernel = lambda u: np.multiply.outer(np.exp(-u), identity)   # vectorized, see above

# Two right-hand sides (m = 2), stacked column-wise into a (d, m) array.
def g(t):
    g0 = np.array([np.sin(t), np.cos(t)])
    g1 = np.array([t, 1.0 + 0.0 * t])
    return np.column_stack([g0, g1])   # shape (d, m)

mesh = np.linspace(0, 1, 21)
y_arr, y = function_solve_VIE_2(
    kernel=kernel, g=g, mesh_breakpoints=mesh,
    coll_divs=2, coll_choices=[0, 1, 2],
    return_function=True,
)

print(y_arr.shape)              # (M, p, d, m) == (20, 3, 2, 2)
print(y(0.5).shape)             # (d, m) == (2, 2)
print(y(np.linspace(0, 1, 5)).shape)  # (len(array), d, m) == (5, 2, 2)

A 2-D g(t) return (or a 2-D soln_init_value for function_solve_VIDE) selects the matrix-valued case; matrix problems require a (d, d) matrix kernel. Complex kernels, g, a, and initial values are supported here too.

The same function_solve_VIE_1, function_solve_VIDE entry points exist with the analogous API. function_solve_VIDE additionally takes an a callable and a required soln_init_value. function_solve_VIE_1 adds the optional force_continuous mode (whose soln_init_value is (d, m) in the matrix case).

docs.title: Example: Vector- and Matrix-Valued Equations
docs.text:
All solvers can solve for vector-valued and matrix-valued functions \(y(t)\). When \(y(t)\) is a \(d\)-dimensional vector, \(g(t)\) is also a \(d\)-dimensional vector and \(K(t)\) and \(a(t)\) are \(d \times d\) matrices. When \(y(t)\) is a \(d \times m\) matrix, \(g(t)\) is also a \(d \times m\) matrix and \(K(t)\) and \(a(t)\) are \(d \times d\) matrices.

The case is detected automatically: for the array-based family from the shapes of the input arrays, and for the callable family from the shape returned by g(t) (a (d, m) return — or a (d, m) soln_init_value for VIDE — selects the matrix case). The callable family builds the kernel weight tensor once and shares it across the \(m\) columns, so a matrix solve is much cheaper than \(m\) separate calls; see the callable-solver examples for a worked case.

docs.title: Array-based 2×2 example
docs.text:
A 2×2 VIE-1 with constant kernel \(K = \begin{bmatrix} 3/2 & -1/2 \\ -1/2 & 3/2 \end{bmatrix}\), \(g(t) = [t + \tfrac{3}{2}t^2,\ t - \tfrac{1}{2}t^2]\), and exact solution \(y(t) = [1 + 2t,\ 1]\):

import numpy as np
from voles import solve_VIE_1

time_step = 0.1
times = np.arange(0, 9.1, time_step)   # 91 pts = 10×3² + 1
N = len(times)

kernel = np.full((N, 2, 2), [[1.5, -0.5], [-0.5, 1.5]])

g = np.zeros((N, 2))
g[:, 0] = times + 1.5 * times**2
g[:, 1] = times - 0.5 * times**2

soln = solve_VIE_1(kernel_values=kernel, g_values=g, time_step=time_step)
# soln shape: (N, 2)
exact = np.column_stack([1 + 2*times, np.ones(N)])
print(f"Max error: {np.max(np.abs(soln - exact)):.2e}")

docs.title: Example: Polynomial Solutions (return_function)
docs.text:
The solvers approximate each component of \(y(t)\) as a piecewise polynomial: the time axis is divided into mesh intervals, and on each interval the solution is an explicit polynomial fixed by requiring the Volterra equation to hold at a set of collocation points within that interval.

Because the solution on each interval is an explicit polynomial, the solver can return it. Passing return_function=True to any solver returns a (soln_values, solution) tuple (return_polys=True is a deprecated alias). solution(t) evaluates the piecewise polynomial at any time in \([0, T]\) (NaN outside), and solution also indexes/iterates like a list of numpy.polynomial.Polynomial objects covering successive mesh intervals — these can be evaluated at any point, differentiated, integrated, and so on.

The following example uses solve_VIDE to solve for \(y(t) = \sin(t)\), then evaluates the solution and its derivative at a point not on the time grid:

import numpy as np
from voles import solve_VIDE

# y(t) = sin(t) satisfies this VIDE with K(u) = exp(-u), a(t) = -1
time_step = 0.1
times = np.arange(0, 8.9, time_step)   # 89 points = 22×2² + 1 (coll_divs=2)
kernel = np.exp(-times)
a = np.full(len(times), -1.0)
g = 1.5*np.cos(times) + 0.5*np.sin(times) - 0.5*np.exp(-times)

soln_vals, solution = solve_VIDE(
    kernel_values=kernel,
    a_values=a,
    g_values=g,
    soln_init_value=0.0,
    time_step=time_step,
    return_function=True,
)

# solution(t) evaluates the piecewise polynomial directly:
print(f"y(0.2)  ≈ {solution(0.2):.6f},  exact = {np.sin(0.2):.6f}")

# solution also indexes like the per-interval polynomials:
p = solution[0]                         # numpy.polynomial.Polynomial on t ∈ [0, 0.4]

# Differentiate to recover y'(t):
print(f"y'(0.2) ≈ {p.deriv()(0.2):.6f},  exact = {np.cos(0.2):.6f}")

docs.title: Example: Product integration for sampled kernels
docs.text:
The array-based solvers take the kernel as samples K(u) on a grid of spacing time_step. With quadrature="collocation" every integral in the collocation equations is evaluated with the interpolatory rule on the collocation nodes themselves (Brunner 2004, Section 2.4.5). That rule needs the kernel at the scaled nodes of each partial interval, which fall on samples only when the mesh is coll_divs**2 samples wide, so:

  • the mesh width is coll_divs**2 * time_step, and at a fixed sampling rate an order-\(m\) method carries an error constant \(\text{coll\_divs}^{2m}\) times larger than the same method on a mesh one sample wide;
  • only every coll_divs-th sample of the data enters the history sums.

quadrature="product" removes the constraint in the classical way (Linz, BIT 11, 1971; de Hoog and Weiss, SIAM J. Numer. Anal. 10, 1973): the kernel is replaced by its piecewise-polynomial interpolant of degree kernel_interp_degree on the data grid (default: the number of collocation nodes) and its products with the collocation polynomial are integrated exactly. The mesh can then be any multiple mesh_samples of coll_divs samples wide, every sample is used, any convergent node set works without the numba fallback, and the FFT-accelerated history of the D extension is still used. Product integration is the default quadrature of all three solvers. The default mesh is the finest one, mesh_samples=coll_divs, for solve_VIE_2 and solve_VIDE; for solve_VIE_1 it stays at coll_divs**2 samples, because inverting a first-kind equation amplifies errors in the data by roughly the inverse of the mesh width (see below). The collocation quadrature remains available as quadrature="collocation"; it runs in compiled code specialised per setting and is a few times faster.

docs.title: A first-kind equation on coarsely sampled data
docs.text:
The Rubin model (a particle at the end of a semi-infinite harmonic chain) has the correlation function \(C(t) = J_1(2t)/t\) and the memory kernel \(\mathcal{K}(t) = -C(t)\), related by \(\dot C(t) = \int_0^t C(t-s)\mathcal{K}(s)ds\). Sampled at time_step = 0.125, about 25 samples per oscillation period, the collocation quadrature puts the order-3 method on a mesh of width 1.125.

import numpy as np
from scipy.special import j1, jv
from voles import solve_VIE_1

time_step = 0.125
num_pts = 32 * 3**2 + 1                      # valid for both quadratures
times = time_step * np.arange(num_pts)
with np.errstate(all="ignore"):
    C = j1(2 * times) / times                # kernel
    C_dot = -2 * jv(2, 2 * times) / times    # right-hand side
    K_exact = -j1(2 * times) / times
C[0], C_dot[0], K_exact[0] = 1.0, 0.0, -1.0

common = dict(kernel_values=C, g_values=C_dot, time_step=time_step,
              coll_divs=3, coll_choices=[1, 2, 3], show_warnings=False)

K_coll = solve_VIE_1(quadrature="collocation", **common)       # mesh 9 samples wide
K_prod = solve_VIE_1(mesh_samples=3, **common)                  # product: mesh 3 samples wide

err_coll = np.max(np.abs(K_coll - K_exact))
err_prod = np.max(np.abs(K_prod - K_exact))
print(f"collocation quadrature: max error {err_coll:.1e}")
print(f"product integration:    max error {err_prod:.1e}")
assert err_prod < err_coll / 10

mesh_samples chooses the mesh explicitly. With mesh_samples=9 the mesh is the same as the collocation quadrature's, but the integrals now use all nine samples of each interval rather than three of them:

import numpy as np
from scipy.special import j1, jv
from voles import solve_VIE_1

time_step = 0.125
times = time_step * np.arange(32 * 9 + 1)
with np.errstate(all="ignore"):
    C = j1(2 * times) / times
    C_dot = -2 * jv(2, 2 * times) / times
    K_exact = -j1(2 * times) / times
C[0], C_dot[0], K_exact[0] = 1.0, 0.0, -1.0

K_prod9 = solve_VIE_1(kernel_values=C, g_values=C_dot, time_step=time_step,
                      coll_divs=3, coll_choices=[1, 2, 3],
                      quadrature="product", mesh_samples=9, show_warnings=False)
print(f"product integration, mesh_samples=9: max error "
      f"{np.max(np.abs(K_prod9 - K_exact)):.1e}")

Any input length of at least mesh_samples + 1 is accepted; as for the default quadrature, leftover samples past the last regular mesh interval are absorbed by stretching that interval, so the solution covers every sample.

Noisy data and first-kind equations. Inverting a first-kind equation amplifies errors in the data by roughly the inverse of the mesh width, so on noisy data the finest mesh is not automatically the best choice. mesh_samples is the knob: larger values trade resolution for a milder amplification. The second-kind equation and the VIDE below are well posed and have no such trade-off.

docs.title: Propagating with a sampled kernel: the VIDE
docs.text:
The same keywords apply to solve_VIE_2 and solve_VIDE. Here the memory kernel \(K(u) = -e^{-u/2}\) is sampled and the correlation function is propagated forward from \(y(0) = 1\); the exact solution satisfies \(y'' + y'/2 + y = 0\).

import numpy as np
from voles import solve_VIDE

time_step = 0.1
num_pts = 20 * 3**2 + 1
times = time_step * np.arange(num_pts)
kernel = -np.exp(-times / 2)
omega = np.sqrt(1 - 1 / 16)
exact = np.exp(-times / 4) * (np.cos(omega * times) + np.sin(omega * times) / (4 * omega))

common = dict(kernel_values=kernel, soln_init_value=1.0, time_step=time_step,
              coll_divs=3, coll_choices=[1, 2, 3], show_warnings=False)
y_coll = solve_VIDE(quadrature="collocation", **common)
y_prod = solve_VIDE(**common)                       # product integration is the default

err_coll = np.max(np.abs(y_coll - exact))
err_prod = np.max(np.abs(y_prod - exact))
print(f"collocation quadrature: max error {err_coll:.1e}")
print(f"product integration:    max error {err_prod:.1e}")
assert err_prod < err_coll / 5

Because product integration evaluates the weights in Python from the samples and only needs the D extension for the stepping, node sets that are not compiled into the extension are also available:

import numpy as np
from voles import solve_VIDE

time_step = 0.1
times = time_step * np.arange(20 * 5 + 1)
kernel = -np.exp(-times / 2)
y5 = solve_VIDE(quadrature="product", kernel_values=kernel, soln_init_value=1.0,
                time_step=time_step, coll_divs=5, coll_choices=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5],
                show_warnings=False)
omega = np.sqrt(1 - 1 / 16)
exact = np.exp(-times / 4) * (np.cos(omega * times) + np.sin(omega * times) / (4 * omega))
assert np.max(np.abs(y5 - exact)) < 1e-4

docs.title: Example: Volterra Integro-Differential Equation
docs.text:
Solve the VIDE

\[y'(t) = a(t)y(t) + g(t) + \int_0^t K(t-s)y(s)ds\]

with \(a(t) = \frac{1}{1+t^2}\), \(K(u) = e^{-u}\), and \(g(t)\) chosen so the exact solution is \(y(t) = \sin(t)\).

import numpy as np
from voles import solve_VIDE

time_step = 0.01
coll_divs = 3
num_pts = 10 * coll_divs**2 + 1   # 91
times = np.array([i * time_step for i in range(num_pts)])

kernel = np.exp(-times)
a = 1.0 / (1.0 + times**2)
g = (np.cos(times)
     - 0.5 * (np.exp(-times) + np.sin(times) - np.cos(times))
     - np.sin(times) / (1.0 + times**2))

soln_vals, solution = solve_VIDE(
    g_values=g,
    kernel_values=kernel,
    a_values=a,
    soln_init_value=0.0,   # sin(0) = 0
    coll_divs=coll_divs,
    coll_choices=[1, 2, 3],
    time_step=time_step,
    return_function=True,
)

exact = np.sin(times)
print(f"Max error: {np.max(np.abs(soln_vals - exact)):.2e}")
assert np.max(np.abs(soln_vals - exact)) < 1e-3

# `solution` is callable at any time in [0, T], and also indexes/iterates like the
# per-interval polynomials (solution[n], for poly in solution, ...).
print(f"y(0.5) = {solution(0.5):.6f}  (exact {np.sin(0.5):.6f})")

docs.title: Example: Type-1 Volterra Integral Equation
docs.text:
Solve the VIE-1

\[g(t) = \int_0^t K(t-s)y(s)ds\]

with \(K(u) = e^u\) (as a function of the lag \(u = t - s\)), \(g(t) = \sin(t)\), whose exact solution is \(y(t) = \cos(t) - \sin(t)\).

import numpy as np
from voles import solve_VIE_1

time_step = 0.01
coll_divs = 3
num_pts = 10 * coll_divs**2 + 1   # 91
times = np.array([i * time_step for i in range(num_pts)])

kernel = np.exp(times)
g = np.sin(times)
g[0] = 0.0

sol_vals, solution = solve_VIE_1(
    g_values=g,
    kernel_values=kernel,
    coll_divs=coll_divs,
    coll_choices=[1, 2, 3],
    time_step=time_step,
    return_function=True,
)

exact = np.cos(times) - np.sin(times)
print(f"Max error: {np.max(np.abs(sol_vals - exact)):.2e}")
assert np.max(np.abs(sol_vals - exact)) < 1e-3

# `solution` is callable at any time in [0, T], and also indexes/iterates like the
# per-interval polynomials (solution[n], for poly in solution, ...).
exact_at = np.cos(0.5) - np.sin(0.5)
print(f"y(0.5) = {solution(0.5):.6f}  (exact {exact_at:.6f})")
